revisions.objective: Own the weight-gradient kernel and its use of scratch in src/candidate.cu. Compare reduction granularities rather than assuming multi-stage partial sums win: test a CTA-level reduction distributed across B*L for each (h,j), and, where useful, split B*L into tiles that write partial sums to scratch followed by a final reduction. You may also test tiling neighboring j outputs if it enables useful reuse. Use no extra allocations; every scratch read must follow a write in the current call, and all outputs must be freshly written. Preserve bounds, the contracted gradient, full FP32, and the required tolerances for all valid inputs. Judge variants by correctness and complete-call timing, since the supplied baseline timing does not attribute cost to this kernel.

data.shared_assumptions: The supplied baseline is correct at 35.464 ms mean across three end-to-end samples, but offers no per-kernel breakdown. Source inspection suggests the separate forward/input-gradient launches use one 256-thread CTA per (b,h) row at L=48, with 48 useful threads, while the weight-gradient path serially traverses B*L per output; actual costs remain unmeasured. T1 versus T2 is a deliberate separate-versus-fused comparison. All trees must preserve full FP32, all-input correctness and fresh writes; scratch is uninitialized and may only be read after being written in the call. Use official complete-call measurements and validation; final G still needs independent confirmation.
